The sauce will seem too thick initially — keep tossing for a full minute as it loosens from the noodle starch. Pile into bowls and top with the cucumber julienne and scallion. The cucumber should sit on top, not mixed in, so it stays crisp. Drizzle with extra chili oil if desired. Serve at room temperature — do not refrigerate before serving.
fr-coleslaw: Combine the shredded green cabbage, red cabbage, and grated carrots in a large colander set over a bowl. Toss with 1 teaspoon of the kosher salt from the seasoning allotment. Let stand for 30 minutes — the salt will draw out the cabbage's excess water through osmosis. Rinse briefly under cold water, then squeeze firmly with your hands or press between two clean kitchen towels to remove as much liquid as possible.

In a medium bowl, whisk together the mayonnaise, apple cider vinegar, sugar, celery seed, remaining salt, and a generous crack of black pepper until smooth and fully combined. Taste the dressing before adding it to the cabbage — it should taste tangier and saltier than you want the final slaw, because the cabbage will dilute it. Adjust the balance of vinegar and sugar to your preference.

Add the squeezed-dry cabbage mixture to the dressing and toss thoroughly until every strand is coated. Taste and adjust seasoning. Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour before serving — ideally 2 hours. The resting time is not optional: it allows the dressing to penetrate the cabbage, the flavors to meld, and the texture to achieve the perfect balance of crisp and tender.

Remove the slaw from the refrigerator 10 minutes before serving. Toss once more and taste for a final seasoning adjustment — cold suppresses flavor, so it may need a pinch more salt or a splash more vinegar after the chill. Serve cold alongside BBQ or fried chicken. Transfer to a serving bowl with tongs, allowing the excess dressing to drain in the bowl.
fr-confit-canard: Score the duck skin in a crosshatch pattern with a sharp knife, cutting through the fat but not into the meat. Rub each leg all over with coarse salt, then press thyme, bay, and garlic against the skin. Stack in a non-reactive container, cover, and refrigerate for 12–24 hours. The salt will draw moisture from the skin, concentrating flavour and improving the final crispness.

Melt the duck fat in a deep, heavy pot. Pat the rinsed duck legs completely dry. Submerge them fully in the fat — add more fat if needed to cover. Heat until the fat reaches 80–90 C (175–195 F). Maintain this temperature in a 90 C (195 F) oven for 6–8 hours. The fat should show only the most occasional lazy bubble — a trembling rather than a simmer. At this temperature, the collagen converts to gelatin without the muscle fibers seizing up.

Remove the duck legs from the fat (reserving all fat for storage and future cooking). Pat the skin completely dry with paper towels. Heat an oven-safe pan over high heat until smoking. Place the duck legs skin-side down with no additional fat. Press gently to ensure full skin contact. Sear for 4–6 minutes without moving until the skin is deeply golden-brown and crackling audibly. Transfer to a 220 C (430 F) oven skin-side up for 5 more minutes to heat through.
fr-confit-garlic: Peel the garlic cloves individually, keeping them whole and intact — any nick or cut will cause the clove to break down prematurely in the oil and cloud it. Discard any that are bruised or have gone soft. If any have a green sprout in the center, split the clove and remove it — the sprout is bitter and will muddy the finished oil. Pat the peeled cloves completely dry with paper towels. Place them in a small, heavy-based saucepan — they should fit in a single close layer. A vessel that is too large requires excessive oil to submerge them.

Pour enough olive oil over the garlic cloves to submerge them by 1–2cm. Add the thyme, bay leaf and peppercorns. Set the pan over the lowest possible heat on your smallest burner. Bring the oil to 85–90°C — use a thermometer; this is the critical range. The oil should show tiny, lazy bubbles rising occasionally from the garlic, like a very gentle spring rather than a simmer. Too hot (above 100°C) and you are frying the garlic, which will brown and turn acrid. Too cool and the collagen won't break down and the cloves won't turn silky. Maintain this gentle warmth, checking occasionally, for 45–60 minutes. The cloves are done when they can be pierced easily with a cake tester and have turned a very pale, golden-ivory colour throughout.

Remove the pan from the heat and let the garlic cool completely in its oil — do not attempt to transfer while hot. Once cooled, transfer the cloves and oil together to a sterilised glass jar, ensuring all cloves are completely submerged in oil. They will keep refrigerated for up to 2 weeks. Use the cloves whole, mashed onto toast, stirred into gluten-free pasta or mashed potato, or dissolved into sauces. Use the perfumed oil for salad dressings, gluten-free pasta, roasting vegetables, drizzling over soups — it is possibly more versatile than the cloves themselves. Never store confit garlic at room temperature for extended periods (the anaerobic, low-acid environment creates a botulism risk).
fr-congee: Rinse the rice in cold water two or three times, swirling with your hand, until the water runs from milky to nearly clear — but stop before it is perfectly clear, as some surface starch helps the porridge thicken. Drain well, then rub the rice with the neutral oil and half the salt. Let it sit for 15-30 minutes. The oil coats each grain so it breaks down evenly and gives the finished congee a glossy sheen.

Bring the water (or stock) and ginger coins to a rolling boil in a tall, heavy pot. Add the primed rice and stir once from the bottom to lift any grains stuck to the base. Let it return to a vigorous boil for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. This initial hard boil cracks the grains open and starts releasing their starch into the water.

Reduce to a low, steady simmer and set the lid slightly ajar. Cook for 60-75 minutes, stirring every 10-15 minutes to keep the rice from settling and catching on the bottom. The grains will swell, split, and finally dissolve, thickening the liquid into a smooth, pourable porridge. Stir more often toward the end as it thickens. If it grows too thick, loosen with a splash of hot water.

Taste and adjust with a few drops of tamari and a pinch of white pepper — congee should be gently seasoned, a quiet base rather than a bold dish. Ladle the hot porridge into warm bowls. Scatter sliced scallions and fried shallots over the top, and finish each bowl with another tiny crack of white pepper. Serve immediately while it steams.
fr-couscous-seven-vegetables: Heat the olive oil in a large, wide pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and golden at the edges, about 8 minutes. Stir in the tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes until it darkens. Add the ras el hanout, turmeric and cinnamon and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Bloom the saffron in a tablespoon of warm water and add it to the pot. Add the carrots, turnips and chickpeas, pour in the water, and season generously with salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a steady simmer and cook 20 minutes — these harder vegetables go in first because they need the most time.

While the stew base simmers, place the dry couscous in a large bowl. Sprinkle over 1 teaspoon of salt, then drizzle with 3 tablespoons of cold water and 1 tablespoon of olive oil. Rub the grains between your palms to distribute the moisture evenly and break up any clumps. If you have a couscoussier or large steamer, line it with a damp cloth and add the couscous. Steam over the simmering stew (or plain boiling water) for 15 minutes. The steam perfumes the couscous with the stew's aromatics.

Tip the first-steamed couscous into a large bowl. Add the butter and a ladleful of the hot stew broth. Rake vigorously with your fingers or a large fork, breaking up every clump and coating each grain in the butter and broth. Taste and add more salt if needed. Return to the steamer for a second 15-minute steam. Meanwhile, add the butternut squash, zucchini and cabbage to the stew and continue simmering for the remaining 20–25 minutes until all vegetables are tender and the broth has reduced slightly and thickened.

Mound the finished couscous in a high dome on a large round platter or communal bowl. Ladle the vegetable stew with all its vegetables over and around the couscous, allowing the broth to soak into the center of the mound. Scatter chopped cilantro over the top. Serve the remaining hot broth in a small jug on the side for people to add as they eat. Serve the harissa in a separate small dish. Traditionally this is eaten communally, everyone gathering around the shared platter.

fr-crab-cakes: In a large bowl, whisk together the beaten egg, mayonnaise, Old Bay, Dijon mustard, and chopped parsley until smooth and uniform. This is the entire binding and seasoning base — taste it on a cracker to calibrate the salt and spice before it touches the crab. The mixture should taste bright, slightly sharp from the mustard, and warmly spiced.

Add the crab meat and breadcrumbs to the binder. Using a large spatula or clean hands, fold very gently — five to eight slow, sweeping folds maximum. The goal is to coat the crab in the binder while leaving the lumps as intact as possible. Every time you stir, you break crab. Stop the moment the mixture barely holds together. It should look loose and shaggy, not smooth and paste-like.

Divide the mixture into six equal portions (roughly 100–120 g each). Gently press each into a thick disc about 4 cm high — do not compress too firmly. Place on a parchment-lined tray and refrigerate uncovered for 30 minutes minimum, up to 4 hours. The cold firms the binder and makes the patties dramatically easier to flip without falling apart in the pan.

Heat a heavy skillet (cast iron or stainless) over medium heat. Add the butter and oil together — the oil raises the smoke point, the butter brings color and flavor. When the butter foam subsides and the fat shimmers, carefully lower the patties in, leaving space between them. Do not move them. Cook 3–4 minutes per side. Resist flipping early — they will release cleanly once a golden crust has formed. Use a thin fish spatula and flip once only.

Transfer to warm plates immediately — do not rest them on a rack or they will steam and soften the crust. Serve with lemon wedges and a remoulade or simple tartar sauce alongside. The cakes are best eaten within two minutes of leaving the pan, while the contrast between the crisp exterior and the barely-bound interior is at its peak.

fr-creamy-lemon-spinach-chicken-pasta: Bring about 4 l (4 qt) water to a boil in a large pot and add the salt. Cook the pasta 1 minute less than the package directions, stirring in the first minute. Before draining, scoop out a mug of the starchy cooking water (you need about 180 ml), then drain.

While the water heats, pat the chicken dry and season with 3/4 tsp kosher salt and pepper. Heat the oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chicken in a single layer and cook without stirring 3 minutes until golden underneath, then turn and cook 2–3 minutes more until cooked through to 165°F (74°C) — check the largest piece. Transfer to a plate.

Lower the heat to medium, add the butter to the same skillet and, once it foams, add the garlic and pepper flakes; cook 45 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the cream and the lemon zest, scraping up the browned bits, and simmer gently 2–3 minutes until slightly thickened.

Add the drained pasta and 120 ml of the pasta water to the skillet and toss over medium-low heat for 1–2 minutes until the pasta is al dente and the sauce clings. Take off the heat, add the Parmesan in handfuls, tossing to melt, then add the spinach and chicken and toss until the spinach just wilts. Stir in 2 tbsp lemon juice, taste, and add more lemon, salt, pepper or a splash of pasta water to loosen. Serve immediately.

fr-crema-catalana: Combine the whole milk with the cinnamon stick and lemon zest in a heavy-bottomed saucepan. Set over medium heat and bring slowly to a bare simmer — small bubbles forming at the edge, not a rolling boil. Remove from heat the moment it steams and the first bubbles appear. Cover the pot and let it steep for 20 minutes off the heat. The milk will absorb the fragrant oils from the lemon zest and the warm spice of the cinnamon, building the aromatic base that defines crema catalana from crème brûlée. Strain the milk through a fine sieve to remove the zest and cinnamon, pressing lightly to extract the flavored oils. The milk should smell unmistakably of warm citrus and spice.

In a large bowl, whisk the egg yolks with the caster sugar until the mixture turns pale, thick, and ribbony — lift the whisk and the mixture should fall back in a slow, fat ribbon that holds its shape for 2–3 seconds before dissolving. This takes about 3 minutes of vigorous whisking. Then whisk in the cornstarch until no dry lumps remain. The cornstarch is what differentiates crema catalana from a pure yolk custard — it gives a firmer, slightly starchier set that holds up in the shallow terracotta dishes and allows the crust to be applied without the custard collapsing. Do not skip this step or substitute with flour.

Reheat the strained infused milk over medium heat until it's steaming and just below a simmer. Slowly pour a small ladle of hot milk into the yolk mixture while whisking constantly — this is the temper, which raises the egg temperature gently without scrambling. Pour in a second ladle, then return the entire mixture to the saucepan. Cook over medium-low heat, whisking constantly and making sure to cover every part of the bottom and corners of the pan. The custard will thicken quickly — within 3–4 minutes it will begin to coat the back of a spoon. As soon as it thickens noticeably and the first large bubble pops at the surface, remove from heat. The cornstarch needs to reach just past gelatinization temperature, which happens around the first boil. Pour immediately into shallow terracotta or ramekin dishes. Chill uncovered for at least 3 hours until completely cold and set.

Remove the chilled custard dishes from the refrigerator. Sprinkle an even, thin layer of caster sugar over each custard — about 1 teaspoon per 10 cm dish — and tilt the dish to spread it uniformly to the edges with no bare patches and no thick mounds. The sugar must be dry and even, like a thin sheet of paper. Traditionally crema catalana is finished with a red-hot iron (ferro), but a kitchen torch works perfectly: hold the flame 2–3 cm from the surface and move in tight circles, watching the sugar melt, bubble, and caramelize from the center outward to the edges. Stop the moment the surface turns amber-brown — it continues to darken for a second after the flame moves away. The crema should be served within 10 minutes of caramelizing, before the sugar absorbs moisture and softens.
fr-creme-caramel: Combine the caramel sugar and water in a small, light-colored saucepan. Stir once to dissolve, then stop stirring entirely. Place over medium-high heat. The sugar will bubble, then color. Swirl the pan gently — never stir — to ensure even browning. Remove from heat when it reaches a deep amber. Immediately pour into ramekins and swirl to coat the bottoms.

Combine milk with the split vanilla bean and its scraped seeds in a saucepan. Heat over medium until steam rises and small bubbles form at the edge — do not boil. Remove from heat, cover, and let the vanilla steep for 15 minutes. Remove the vanilla pod.

Whisk eggs and custard sugar together gently — combine them without creating foam. Slowly pour the warm milk into the egg mixture in a thin stream, whisking constantly. This tempers the eggs so they do not scramble. Strain the custard through a fine-mesh sieve into a pouring vessel. Let any bubbles settle for 5 minutes.

Pour custard into caramel-lined ramekins, filling to 5mm below the rim. Place ramekins in a deep baking dish and pour hot water into the dish until it reaches halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Bake at 150 C (300 F) for 50-60 minutes. The water bath insulates the custard from direct heat, preventing curdling.

Cool ramekins to room temperature, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight. To unmold: run a thin knife around the edge, place a plate on top, and invert confidently in one motion. The caramel will have liquefied in the fridge and will pour down the sides as a sauce.
fr-creme-patissiere: Split the vanilla bean lengthwise, scrape out the seeds, and add both pod and seeds to the milk in a medium saucepan. Heat over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the milk just reaches a simmer — small bubbles at the edges, steam rising. Remove from heat, cover, and steep for 10 minutes to deepen the vanilla infusion. Remove the pod (rinse and dry it for vanilla sugar).

In a large bowl, whisk the egg yolks and sugar together vigorously for 1–2 minutes until the mixture is pale, thick, and forms a ribbon. Sift in the cornflour and whisk again until completely smooth with no lumps. This paste must be completely lump-free or the finished cream will have starchy pockets.

Pour a ladleful of the hot infused milk into the egg yolk paste, whisking constantly and vigorously to raise the temperature of the yolks gently without scrambling them. Once combined, pour in the remaining hot milk in a slow, steady stream while whisking. Return the entire mixture to the saucepan.

Return the custard to the saucepan and cook over medium heat, whisking constantly and reaching into every corner of the pan. The mixture will first appear to thicken slightly, then will suddenly seize up and become very thick — keep whisking as it crosses from liquid to thick paste. This is the starch gelatinising. Crucially, once the cream has thickened, continue cooking at a full boil for 1–2 minutes, whisking hard, to cook out the raw starch flavour. Remove from heat, beat in the cold butter, and press cling film directly onto the surface. Refrigerate until cold and firm (at least 1.5 hours).
fr-crepes-suzette: Whisk the flour, sugar and salt in a bowl, make a well, and crack in the eggs. Whisk from the centre outward, drawing in the flour, then pour in the milk in a slow stream to keep the batter lump-free. Whisk in the cooled browned butter. The batter should be thin — the consistency of single cream. Strain it through a sieve and rest, covered, in the fridge for at least 30 minutes to let the gluten relax and the bubbles settle.

Heat a 22 cm crêpe or non-stick pan over medium heat and wipe it with a film of butter. Lift the pan, ladle in just enough batter to coat the base, and immediately swirl it into a thin, even round, pouring any excess back. Cook 45-60 seconds until the edges lift and the underside is lacy and golden, then flip and cook 20-30 seconds more. Stack the finished crêpes on a plate as you go; the first one is always the test.

Zest the oranges and squeeze the juice. In a wide skillet, melt the sauce sugar over medium heat without stirring, swirling the pan as it liquefies, until it turns a clear amber caramel. Stand back and carefully pour in the orange juice — it will sputter and seize — then add the zest and simmer, stirring, until the hardened caramel dissolves back into a smooth, syrupy sauce.

Drop the heat to low. Whisk the cold cubed butter into the warm orange caramel a few pieces at a time, letting each addition melt and emulsify before adding more. The sauce should turn satiny, opaque and slightly thickened — a true beurre Suzette. Keep it just warm; do not let it boil hard or the butter will split and the sauce will turn greasy.

One at a time, lay each crêpe in the warm sauce, turn to coat both sides, then fold in half and in half again into a neat triangle, nudging it to the side of the pan. Repeat until all the crêpes are folded and overlapping in the sauce, basting them with a spoon so each absorbs the orange-butter and glistens.

Off the heat, pour the Grand Marnier over the crêpes. Return the pan to the flame and tilt it slightly toward the burner (or touch a long match to the edge) so the warmed alcohol vapour catches and bursts into blue flame. Let it burn down on its own, swirling the pan, until the flames die and the sauce reduces to a final glossy lacquer. Plate the folded crêpes at once and spoon the remaining sauce over the top.

fr-crispy-duck-legs: Score the duck skin in a diagonal crosshatch with a sharp knife, cutting through the skin and fat but not the meat beneath. Rub the legs all over with flaky salt, cracked pepper, and thyme, pressing the herbs into the score marks. Tuck garlic halves and bay leaves under and around the legs in a dish. Refrigerate uncovered overnight (8–12 hours). The salt draws moisture from the skin and seasons the meat throughout.

Place duck legs skin-side down in a cold, dry, oven-proof skillet or roasting pan. Do not preheat — starting cold prevents the skin from buckling. Place in a cold oven and turn to 130 C (260 F). Cook for 3–4 hours, skin-side down the entire time. The duck fat will render out gradually; the legs will sit in an increasing pool of their own golden fat. Occasionally tilt the pan and spoon off excess fat.

Pour off most of the rendered fat into a jar to save. Increase oven to 220 C (425 F) or, for maximum control, transfer legs to a fresh skillet and crisp skin-side down on the stovetop over medium-high heat for 5–8 minutes. Watch attentively — the goal is a shattering, golden-mahogany skin, not burnt. Flip for a final 2 minutes on the meat side.

Rest the duck legs for 3 minutes — just enough for carryover cooking to complete, not long enough for the skin to steam and soften. Sprinkle with fleur de sel and fresh thyme leaves. Serve skin-side up, immediately, with lentils du Puy, sautéed wild mushrooms, or a bitter green salad dressed with the rendered duck fat.
fr-crispy-pork-belly: Using a metal skewer or a fork, prick the skin of the pork belly hundreds of times over its entire surface, going about 5mm deep but not piercing through to the fat layer. Flip the belly and score the meat side in a crosshatch pattern, 2cm deep. This mechanical disruption of the skin creates channels for rendered fat to escape during roasting, which is what causes the skin to blister and shatter.

Flip the belly meat-side up. Rub the five-spice powder, minced garlic, white pepper, and half the salt thoroughly into the meat and into all the score cuts — get the seasoning as deep into the cuts as possible. Flip skin-side up and rub the remaining salt onto the skin evenly. Place skin-side up, uncovered, in the refrigerator for a minimum of 6 hours or overnight. The desiccating air of the refrigerator is what drives the final moisture out of the skin.

Dissolve the baking soda in rice vinegar and brush onto the skin generously; the alkalinity raises the pH of the skin, accelerating the Maillard reaction and driving crisping. Place skin-side up on a wire rack over a foil-lined tray. Roast at 180°C (360°F) for 50 minutes to render the fat, then blast at 230°C (450°F) for 20–25 minutes for the crackling. Watch closely in the final stage — the transformation from rendered to blistered is fast.

Remove from the oven and rest on the wire rack — never on a flat surface which would trap steam and soften the crackling. Rest for 10 minutes before slicing. Slice using a sharp cleaver or heavy chef's knife with downward pressure rather than sawing; sawing shatters the crackling unevenly.
fr-crispy-tofu-lettuce-cups: Pat the pressed tofu dry and crumble it with your fingers into pea- to chickpea-sized pieces. Heat 30 ml of the oil in a large nonstick skillet or wok over medium-high heat until shimmering (about 350°F / 175°C). Add the tofu in an even layer and cook 10–12 minutes, stirring only every 2 minutes, until the water has cooked off and the crumbles are golden and crisp. Drizzle in 1 tablespoon of the soy sauce for the final minute and toss until absorbed. Transfer to a plate.

Add the remaining 15 ml oil to the same pan over high heat. Add the shiitake and cook 3–4 minutes until they release their moisture and brown. Add the garlic, ginger, and scallion whites and stir-fry 45 seconds until fragrant, then add the water chestnuts and toss 1 minute to heat through.

Stir together the remaining soy sauce, hoisin, rice vinegar, sriracha, and sesame oil. Return the tofu to the pan, pour in the sauce, and toss over high heat for 1–2 minutes until the sauce reduces and clings to every crumble. Take off the heat.
Arrange the chilled lettuce leaves cup-side up on a platter. Spoon in the hot filling, then top with carrot matchsticks, scallion greens, and cashews. Serve with lime wedges to squeeze over.

Arrange the chilled lettuce leaves cup-side up on a platter. Spoon in the hot filling, then top with carrot matchsticks, scallion greens, and sunflower seeds. Serve with lime wedges to squeeze over.
fr-crispy-tofu-peanut-noodles: Wrap the tofu block in a clean towel and press under a heavy pan for 15 minutes. Cut into 2 cm cubes, sprinkle with a pinch of salt, then toss in a bowl with the cornstarch until every face is dusted. Shake off any clumps.

Heat the oil in a 30 cm nonstick or well-seasoned skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers (about 350°F / 175°C). Add the tofu in a single layer with space between cubes. Fry 3–4 minutes per side, turning with tongs, for 10–12 minutes total, until golden and crisp on at least four faces. Drain on a paper-towel-lined plate.

In a large bowl that will hold the noodles, whisk the peanut butter, soy sauce, rice vinegar, lime juice, maple syrup, garlic, ginger, chili crisp, and sesame oil into a thick paste. It will seize and look stiff at first — that's normal; it loosens with hot water in the next step.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil (212°F / 100°C). Cook the noodles according to the package, usually 4–6 minutes, until just tender with a little chew. Scoop out 120 ml of the cooking water before draining. Rinse briefly under warm water to remove surface starch, then drain well.

Whisk the hot noodle water into the sauce a splash at a time until it pours like heavy cream. Add the noodles and toss with tongs for about 1 minute until every strand is coated. Divide into bowls and top with crispy tofu, cucumber, scallions, peanuts, and cilantro. Add the tofu last so it stays crisp.

fr-croque-monsieur: Melt butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add flour all at once and stir vigorously with a wooden spoon or whisk for 90 seconds — the roux should turn pale blonde and smell faintly nutty, not raw. Gradually pour in warm milk, whisking constantly to prevent lumps. Stir over medium heat until the sauce thickens to a consistency that coats the back of a spoon heavily. Season with salt, white pepper, and a generous grating of nutmeg.

Spread butter on one side of each bread slice. Toast buttered-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat for 2–3 minutes until golden and fragrant. This step is often skipped in shortcuts, but pre-toasting prevents the bottom bread from going soggy under the wet béchamel. Remove from heat.

Spread a generous layer of béchamel on the untoasted side of the bottom bread slice. Lay ham slices to cover completely. Add a layer of grated Gruyère. Place the second slice on top, toasted side up. Spread more béchamel over the top of the sandwich — this is the defining move of the croque-monsieur — and pile the remaining Gruyère on top.

Place the assembled croque on a baking sheet under a hot broiler set to high, positioned 15 cm from the element. Broil for 3–5 minutes, watching constantly, until the Gruyère on top is bubbling, golden-brown, and developing dark spots. The edges of the béchamel should be caramelizing. Serve immediately — the crust is best in the first 90 seconds.

fr-cuban-black-beans: If using dried beans (soaked overnight), drain and rinse. Place in a large pot and cover with 8cm of cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook for 60-90 minutes until beans are completely tender throughout — they should crush easily between two fingers. Season with salt only when completely soft; salt added before tenderness toughens the skin and extends cooking time significantly. Reserve 2 cups of the bean cooking liquid before draining.

Heat olive oil in a wide, heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add diced onion and green pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 8-10 minutes until completely soft and beginning to turn golden — the onion should be translucent throughout, not just at the edges. Add garlic and cumin. Cook for another 90 seconds, stirring constantly, until the garlic is fragrant and the cumin blooms in the fat, smelling toasty and warm. The sofrito should look like a thick, golden-green jam.

Add the cooked beans to the sofrito pot along with the reserved cooking liquid. Stir to combine and bring to a simmer. Cook uncovered for 20-30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the liquid has reduced and thickened considerably — it should coat the back of a spoon and look glossy. In the final 2 minutes of cooking, add the vinegar or white wine. Do not cook after adding the vinegar; you want the brightness to be present in the finished dish, not cooked away. Taste and adjust salt.
fr-curried-carrot-lentil-soup: Heat oil in a 5–6 litre pot over medium heat. Add cumin seeds and let them sizzle 20–30 seconds until they darken a shade. Add onion with a pinch of salt and cook 7–8 minutes until soft and golden at the edges. Stir in garlic, ginger, and curry powder and cook 60 seconds, stirring constantly.

Add carrots, lentils, and stock. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then simmer partially covered 25–30 minutes, stirring the bottom every so often (red lentils sink and catch), until carrots are completely tender and the lentils have dissolved.

Purée with an immersion blender until completely smooth (or blend in batches, filling the jar no more than half full and venting the lid). Stir in coconut milk and warm through without boiling. Add lime juice and salt to taste — usually 1.5–2 tsp. Thin with water to a pourable consistency. Garnish with cilantro and chili flakes. To freeze: cool in shallow containers, refrigerate within 2 hours, and freeze up to 3 months. It sets up thick when cold; loosen with water as it reheats and add fresh lime.
fr-dacquoise: If starting from whole hazelnuts: roast at 175 C (350 F) for 12-15 minutes, rub in a kitchen towel to remove skins, then pulse in a food processor with the icing sugar until fine but not paste. If using pre-ground hazelnut flour: spread on a tray and toast at 160 C for 8-10 minutes, stirring once, until fragrant and lightly golden. Cool completely before using.

In a scrupulously clean, dry bowl, whip egg whites with salt on medium speed until frothy and opaque. Increase to medium-high and add caster sugar one tablespoon at a time over 3-4 minutes. Continue whipping until the meringue is stiff, very glossy, and the sugar is completely dissolved (rub between fingertips — no grittiness). The meringue should stand in firm peaks that do not droop at all.

Sift icing sugar over the toasted hazelnut flour and stir to combine. Working quickly, fold the hazelnut mixture into the meringue in three additions using a large metal spoon or flat spatula. Cut through the center, sweep under, and flip — do not stir in circles. The mixture will deflate somewhat; this is expected. Stop when no streaks of white meringue are visible.

Preheat oven to 150 C (300 F) fan. Draw three 20cm circles on baking paper, flip the paper over. Pipe or spread the batter evenly within the circles to about 1.5cm thick. Bake 30-35 minutes until lightly golden on the surface and firm to the touch. Turn off the oven and prop the door open 2cm; leave the dacquoise inside for 30 minutes to dry out slowly. This gives the characteristic dry crust with chewy interior.

Beat softened butter until very pale and fluffy, about 5 minutes. In a separate bowl, whisk egg yolks until pale. Make a pâte à bombe: boil caster sugar with a little water to 121 C (250 F) soft-ball stage, then pour slowly onto whisking yolks. Whip until cool. Beat the pâte à bombe into the butter gradually, then beat in the praline paste. The buttercream should be smooth, pipeable, and hold a firm peak. Assemble the dacquoise: dacquoise disc, buttercream, dacquoise, buttercream, dacquoise. Chill 1 hour before cutting.

fr-daifuku-mochi: In a microwave-safe bowl, combine mochiko, sugar, and water (add matcha now if using). Whisk until completely smooth and no dry powder remains. The batter will be thin and milky-white.

Loosely cover the bowl with plastic wrap. Microwave on high for 1 minute. Remove, stir vigorously with a wet silicone spatula. Microwave again for 1 minute. Stir again. Microwave for a final 30–60 seconds until the dough is fully translucent and sticky throughout, with no white, raw-looking patches. Alternatively, steam over boiling water for 20 minutes, stirring halfway through.

While the mochi is still warm (it becomes stiffer as it cools — work quickly), portion the bean paste into balls of about 25 g each (roughly 1 tbsp). Set aside. Dust your work surface and hands generously with katakuriko. Divide the mochi into 8–10 equal portions with a bench scraper or oiled scissors. Flatten each piece into a disc 7–8 cm across using fingertips dusted with gluten-free flour or a rolling pin. Place a bean paste ball in the centre, gather the edges of the mochi disc up around it, and pinch firmly to seal the seam.

Rest the completed daifuku at room temperature for 20–30 minutes to allow the surface to dry slightly and the filling to settle. Do not refrigerate — cold hardens mochi to an unpleasant rubbery stiffness. Serve within 8 hours of making; mochi stales quickly at room temperature.
fr-dal-makhani: Rinse the black urad dal and kidney beans under cold water until the water runs clear. Combine in a large bowl, cover with cold water by at least 5 cm, and soak for a minimum of 8 hours or overnight. The dal will swell to nearly double its volume. Drain and discard the soaking water before cooking.

Transfer the drained dal and beans to a heavy pot or pressure cooker. Cover with fresh cold water by 5 cm. If using a pressure cooker, cook on high pressure for 25–30 minutes. If simmering open on the stovetop, bring to a rolling boil, skim any grey foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook 60–90 minutes, adding hot water to keep the dal submerged. The dal and beans must be completely, utterly soft before you combine them with the masala — an underdone dal will never finish cooking properly in the sauce. Reserve the cooking liquid.

In a separate heavy-bottomed pot or karahi, melt half the butter over medium heat. Add cumin seeds and wait 30 seconds until they sputter and darken. Add the onion and cook, stirring frequently, for 12–15 minutes until deep golden-brown — not blond, not pale. Add garlic and ginger; cook 2 minutes until the raw smell disappears. Add Kashmiri chili powder, garam masala, and salt; stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the tomato passata and cook, stirring often and scraping the bottom, for 15–20 minutes. This is the bhuna: the masala must be roasted in the pan until the fat separates and pools at the edges, the tomato turns deep brick-red, and there is no raw tomato smell left. Do not rush.

Add the cooked dal and beans to the bhuna masala, along with enough of the reserved cooking liquid to make a thick but pourable consistency. Stir everything together and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered on the absolute lowest heat — a diffuser helps — for at least 2 hours, stirring every 20 minutes. Four to six hours is better. The dal will deepen from brown to almost black and the flavors will unify. With 15 minutes left, stir in the heavy cream and the remaining butter. Rub the kasuri methi vigorously between your palms to release its oils before crumbling it in. Taste and correct salt. Serve with butter gluten-free flatbread or steamed basmati.
fr-dan-dan-noodles: Heat a wok over high heat until wisps of smoke appear at the rim. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat the surface. Add the ground pork in a single flat layer — resist the urge to stir. Let it cook undisturbed for 60–90 seconds until the bottom develops a crust and begins to release from the wok. Now break it apart and continue cooking, stirring occasionally, until the pork is cooked through and the pieces are individually caramelized and a little crispy — 4–5 minutes total. Push the pork to the sides of the wok. Add the doubanjiang to the hot center and fry it for 60 seconds, stirring, until it darkens and releases its red oil. Add the minced garlic and stir everything together for 30 seconds. Add the rinsed ya cai (or substitute preserved vegetable) and toss together with the pork and paste for 1 minute. The goal is crispy, concentrated, fragrant mince — not moist and soft. Every piece should be individually browned, almost crunchy at the edges, and deeply savory from the fermented paste. This is a topping and a seasoning, not a protein main.

Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a vigorous rolling boil. Cook the noodles according to their type: fresh noodles need only 60–90 seconds; dried thin wheat noodles typically take 3–4 minutes. Test constantly in the last 30 seconds by pulling a strand out and biting through it — you want it cooked through but still with a very slight resistance at the center, slightly firmer than you would eat it plain, because the sauce will continue softening the noodles as you toss them. Before draining, ladle out approximately 100 ml of the cloudy, starchy cooking water and set it aside — this is the binder that will loosen your sauce to the right coating consistency. Drain the noodles quickly, shaking the colander hard to remove as much water as possible. Do not rinse. A rinsed noodle refuses to hold sauce.

In each serving bowl, combine the sesame paste, chili oil (with its red sediment), soy sauce, black vinegar, Sichuan pepper powder, and sugar. Add 2–3 tablespoons of hot noodle cooking water and whisk with a fork or chopstick until the sauce is smooth, homogeneous, and pourable — the sesame paste tends to seize and clump with cold liquids, so the hot starchy water is essential to emulsify it. The finished sauce should be the consistency of heavy cream: fluid but coat the inside of the bowl. Taste it now — it should be intensely seasoned, almost too salty, too spicy, too nutty when tasted alone. It will come into balance once it coats a full portion of noodles. Adjust accordingly: more vinegar for brightness, more chili oil for heat, more sesame paste for richness, more cooking water to loosen.

Add the hot, drained noodles directly into the sauce bowl. Spoon a generous mound of the crispy pork topping onto the noodles without mixing it in yet. Scatter the scallion rings on top. At the table, instruct your diner to toss everything vigorously with chopsticks for 30 seconds before eating — the tossing distributes the sauce evenly, incorporates the pork into every strand, and emulsifies the last of the residual noodle starch into the sauce. This is the 'dan dan' motion the dish is named for: the bouncing, carrying-pole rhythm of street vendors who shook their portable noodle buckets to coat each serving. Each mouthful should deliver noodle, sauce, and pork in roughly equal amounts. Serve immediately — this dish waits for no one.
fr-dashimaki-tamago: Combine the eggs, cold dashi, mirin, usukuchi soy sauce, and salt in a bowl. Beat with chopsticks using a side-to-side cutting motion — the goal is to break yolks and blend thoroughly without beating in air or creating foam. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a pourable container (a measuring jug works perfectly). The sieving removes chalazae and any undissolved white, guaranteeing a silky, lump-free result. The mixture should be a clear, golden amber.

Place the rectangular tamagoyaki pan over medium heat. Soak a folded paper towel in the neutral oil and rub it thoroughly over the entire inner surface — the towel goes back into the bowl for reuse between layers. Heat the pan until a drop of egg mixture sizzles immediately and sets within a second when dropped on the surface. The pan must be hot enough to cook each layer quickly but not so hot the eggs color or bubble before rolling.

Pour one-third of the egg mixture into the pan, tilting to coat the surface with a thin, even layer. As soon as the surface is about 80% set — no longer liquid but not fully dry — use chopsticks or a tamagoyaki spatula to roll the egg toward you from the far edge in 3–4 folds. Push the roll to the far end of the pan. Re-oil the empty space with the paper towel. Pour in the next third of egg mixture, lifting the existing roll briefly so egg slides beneath it. Repeat the roll toward you, incorporating the first log. Oil again, pour the last third, and roll once more. The finished log should have 3 distinct golden layers visible at the ends. Transfer immediately to a sudare (bamboo mat) or parchment paper and roll tightly into a cylinder. Press and hold for 1 minute to set the shape.

Unwrap the tamago and slice crosswise into 2 cm rounds with a sharp, wet knife. Arrange cut-side up to show the spiral. Place a small mound of freshly grated daikon beside each piece. The daikon is not merely garnish — its gentle enzymatic sharpness cleanses the palate between the sweet, custardy bites and balances the mirin's sweetness.
fr-dashimaki-tamago-gf: Combine the eggs, cold dashi, mirin, usukuchi tamari, and salt in a bowl. Beat with chopsticks using a side-to-side cutting motion — the goal is to break yolks and blend thoroughly without beating in air or creating foam. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve into a pourable container (a measuring jug works perfectly). The sieving removes chalazae and any undissolved white, guaranteeing a silky, lump-free result. The mixture should be a clear, golden amber.

Place the rectangular tamagoyaki pan over medium heat. Soak a folded paper towel in the neutral oil and rub it thoroughly over the entire inner surface — the towel goes back into the bowl for reuse between layers. Heat the pan until a drop of egg mixture sizzles immediately and sets within a second when dropped on the surface. The pan must be hot enough to cook each layer quickly but not so hot the eggs color or bubble before rolling.

Pour one-third of the egg mixture into the pan, tilting to coat the surface with a thin, even layer. As soon as the surface is about 80% set — no longer liquid but not fully dry — use chopsticks or a tamagoyaki spatula to roll the egg toward you from the far edge in 3–4 folds. Push the roll to the far end of the pan. Re-oil the empty space with the paper towel. Pour in the next third of egg mixture, lifting the existing roll briefly so egg slides beneath it. Repeat the roll toward you, incorporating the first log. Oil again, pour the last third, and roll once more. The finished log should have 3 distinct golden layers visible at the ends. Transfer immediately to a sudare (bamboo mat) or parchment paper and roll tightly into a cylinder. Press and hold for 1 minute to set the shape.

Unwrap the tamago and slice crosswise into 2 cm rounds with a sharp, wet knife. Arrange cut-side up to show the spiral. Place a small mound of freshly grated daikon beside each piece. The daikon is not merely garnish — its gentle enzymatic sharpness cleanses the palate between the sweet, custardy bites and balances the mirin's sweetness.
fr-deviled-eggs: Bring a pot of water to a full rolling boil. Lower the eggs on a spoon and boil for exactly 11 minutes. Transfer immediately to an ice bath — cold water with as much ice as possible — and leave for 10 full minutes. The ice bath is what makes or breaks the yolk: it stops the carry-over cooking that creates the grey-green sulphur ring. Peel under cold running water, starting from the wide air-pocket end. Store peeled eggs in cold water until ready to use.

Halve the eggs lengthwise with one clean confident cut. Scoop the yolks into a bowl — the whites go on a platter. Press the yolks through a fine-mesh sieve with the back of a spoon (or use a ricer) for the silkiest possible texture. Add the mayonnaise, Dijon, vinegar, salt, and white pepper. Stir vigorously until completely smooth and creamy — not a grain of yolk should be visible. Taste and adjust: it should be noticeably tangy and well-salted. The filling must be bolder than seems right in the bowl — it softens dramatically once it meets the egg white.

Arrange the egg white halves on a serving platter. If they rock, slice a sliver off the rounded bottom to create a flat base. Pat the interiors dry with a corner of paper towel — any moisture will dilute the filling. Pipe or spoon the filling generously into each cavity, mounding it slightly above the rim of the white — a flush fill looks stingy, a generous dome looks abundant. Each half should have an equal, generous fill.

Hold the paprika over each egg from at least 20 cm above and tap the container gently to dust a thin, even veil of red-orange across the surface — not a clump, just a whisper. Scatter the snipped chives across the tray. Serve immediately or refrigerate uncovered for up to 4 hours. Bring to room temperature 20 minutes before serving — cold filling loses much of its tang and creaminess.
fr-doenjang-jjigae: Pour the anchovy-kelp stock into a clay pot (ttukbaegi) or medium heavy saucepan and bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and gochugaru and stir to combine. Now add the doenjang: do not drop it in whole — instead, place it in a fine-mesh strainer set over the simmering broth and press it through with the back of a spoon, or place it directly in the broth and dissolve it by mashing against the side of the pot with a wooden spoon. Undissolved lumps of doenjang will cook unevenly and leave harsh, sharp pockets. Once fully dissolved, taste the broth — it should be assertively savory, slightly pungent, and have a good underlying heat. Adjust with a pinch more doenjang if it tastes flat.

Add the zucchini half-moons and quartered shiitake mushrooms to the doenjang broth. Stir gently to submerge and bring back to a gentle simmer. Cook for 5–7 minutes until the zucchini is just tender — it should offer slight resistance at the center when pressed with a spoon but not be raw or crunchy. The mushrooms will have softened and begun to release their own umami into the broth, deepening it further. Do not overcook the zucchini to mush; it should hold its shape while becoming silky and fully cooked through.

Add the cubed tofu gently to the simmering stew, nestling it between the vegetables without stirring aggressively — tofu is fragile and breaks apart easily, and large intact cubes are part of the visual and textural identity of the dish. Add the scallion lengths. Simmer gently for 3–4 more minutes, just enough for the tofu to heat through completely and absorb some of the broth. The tofu should retain its cube shape; do not stir the stew once the tofu is in, only gently tilt the pot or spoon broth over the top of the tofu cubes to cook the upper surface.

Remove the pot from the heat and drizzle the toasted sesame oil in a thin stream across the surface of the stew. Do not stir it in; let it pool and shimmer on top. Carry the entire pot or clay vessel directly to the table — doenjang jjigae is served bubbling hot, traditionally in a clay pot that retains heat throughout the meal. Set it on a trivet and ladle into individual bowls over steamed rice. The stew should be eaten immediately while piping hot; the flavors are at their most vivid in the first five minutes of serving.

fr-dolmades: If using preserved grape leaves, drain and rinse them under cold water to remove excess brine, separating any that have stuck together. If using fresh leaves, blanch in boiling salted water for 30 seconds until they turn from bright to olive green and become pliable. In either case, sort through the leaves: set aside any that are torn, very small, or have thick, woody stems — these can be used to line the bottom of the pot rather than as wrappers. Trim any tough stems flush with the leaf base using scissors. Stack the prepared leaves shiny side down (the matte, veined side should face up, toward you, because this is the side the filling will be placed on). The leaves should be supple enough to roll without cracking.

In a large bowl, combine the rinsed raw rice, finely diced onion, chopped dill, chopped mint, half the olive oil, half the lemon juice, salt, and pepper. Mix well with your hands, squeezing and turning the mixture until the rice is coated in oil and herb fragrance. Taste the raw mixture — it should taste brightly seasoned, because the rice will absorb flavors as it cooks and the leaf will mute them slightly. The raw rice is used deliberately: it will cook inside the leaf during steaming, absorbing the juices of the herbs and olive oil as it expands. If you pre-cooked the rice, it would turn mushy and glue the dolmades shut. The mixture should feel slightly wet and fragrant, not dry.

Lay a prepared leaf veined-side up (matte side up) on your work surface, with the stem end closest to you. Place a heaped teaspoon (about 15g) of filling on the lower-center of the leaf, roughly where the stem meets the leaf body. Fold the bottom of the leaf up over the filling, then fold in both sides toward the center, and roll forward tightly toward the tip of the leaf. The roll should be firm and compact — a loose dolma will unroll during cooking and a filling that's too sparse will leave empty space. But don't overfill: the rice needs room to expand or it will burst the leaf. Aim for a cigar-shaped roll slightly thicker than your finger. Place each finished dolma seam-side down on a plate as you work.

Line the bottom of a wide, heavy-bottomed pot with the reserved torn or small leaves — this prevents the dolmades from scorching on the pot floor. Arrange the rolled dolmades tightly in a single layer, seam-side down, wedged snugly against each other (they should not rattle if the pot is shaken). If there are more dolmades than fit in one layer, add a second layer perpendicular to the first. Drizzle the remaining olive oil and lemon juice over the top, then add the water or broth. Place an inverted heatproof plate on top of the dolmades and press it down to compact them — this keeps them from unrolling as the rice expands. Cover the pot and cook over medium-low heat for 45–50 minutes. The dolmades are done when the leaves are completely tender and a dolma opened at the center reveals fully cooked, separate (not mushy) rice.
fr-dorayaki: In a medium mixing bowl, whisk eggs with sugar, honey, and mirin until the sugar dissolves and the mixture is pale, fluffy, and increased in volume — about 2 minutes of vigorous whisking. The mixture should form a thick ribbon that holds its shape momentarily when you lift the whisk. This aeration is what gives dorayaki pancakes their characteristic slight bounce and even crumb. Do not underbeat — pale and voluminous is essential.

Sift cake flour over the egg mixture. Dissolve baking soda in cold water and add to the bowl. Fold everything together with a silicone spatula using gentle J-stroke movements — cut down the center, sweep under the bottom, fold over the top. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat. Stop as soon as no dry flour is visible. Overmixing develops gluten and makes the pancakes tough rather than tender. Rest the batter at room temperature for 15 minutes to allow the flour to fully hydrate and the baking soda to activate.

Heat a flat-bottomed non-stick pan or griddle over the lowest possible heat. Brush with the thinnest possible film of oil, then wipe away the excess with a paper towel — you want just enough oil to prevent sticking, not enough to fry. Pour a ladleful of batter (about 60 ml) into the center of the pan from a height of about 5 cm. The batter will spread naturally into a round — do not spread it. Cook until the entire surface has set and the edges look matte and dry, and tiny bubbles are rising and bursting across the surface from edge to edge (2–3 minutes). Flip once with a thin spatula. Cook the second side for 1 minute only — it will be slightly paler than the first side. Stack on a plate covered with a damp towel to keep soft.

Match pancakes into pairs of similar size. Place one pancake flat-side up. Spoon 2–3 tablespoons of anko into the center and spread it gently to within 1 cm of the edge — it will spread further when the top pancake is pressed on. Place the second pancake flat-side down on top. Press lightly at the center so the filling reaches the edges uniformly but does not overflow. The profile should be a gentle dome — thick in the center, tapering to a neat edge. Wrap individually in plastic wrap and rest 30 minutes — the moisture from the filling softens the pancakes further and melds the flavors.

fr-duck-a-lorange: Pat the duck bone-dry inside and out. Prick the skin all over the breast and thighs with a fork held at a shallow angle, piercing the fat layer but not the meat beneath, so the rendering fat has an exit. Season the cavity and skin generously with salt and white pepper and, ideally, leave uncovered in the fridge an hour or more to dry the skin. Tie the legs to draw the bird tight.

Roast breast-up on a rack at 200°C / 400°F. After 25 minutes drop to 170°C / 340°F and continue, tipping out the rendered fat from the tray every 30 minutes (reserve it — it is gold). Roast about 75-90 minutes total, until the skin is deep amber and crisp and the thigh juices run clear. Rest the bird, loosely tented, at least 15 minutes before carving.

In a clean heavy saucepan, melt the sugar over medium heat without stirring, swirling the pan as it liquefies, until it turns a deep amber caramel right at the edge of bitter — this dark caramel is what keeps the sauce from being merely sweet. Off the heat, stand back and pour in the vinegar; it will sputter and seize. Return to low heat and stir until the hardened caramel melts smooth into a syrupy gastrique.

Blanch the orange zest strips in boiling water for a minute to soften their harsh bitterness, then drain. Add the minced shallot to the gastrique and soften briefly, deglaze with the white wine and reduce by half, then pour in the warm brown stock and the orange juice. Simmer and reduce until the sauce lightly naps a spoon, 8-12 minutes, skimming as needed. Stir in the blanched zest.

Off direct high heat, stir the orange liqueur into the sauce and simmer a few seconds to soften its alcohol. Whisk in the cold butter a knob at a time, off the heat, swirling until the sauce turns glossy and silken — do not let it boil or it will split. Taste and correct the salt and the sweet-sour balance. Carve the rested duck, fan the slices, and spoon the warm sauce over and around. Serve at once.
fr-duck-confit: In a small bowl, mix the salt, cracked pepper, and crushed juniper berries. Lay the duck legs skin-side down in a baking dish. Scatter thyme sprigs, crushed bay leaves, and sliced garlic over the flesh side. Rub the salt mixture firmly into both sides, concentrating on the thicker parts of the thigh. Cover tightly with cling film, pressing it against the skin to exclude air. Refrigerate for 12–18 hours. Do not exceed 24 hours or the cure will draw too much moisture and the final texture will be grainy rather than silky.

Remove the legs from the brine and rinse each one thoroughly under cold running water, washing away all the salt, garlic, and herb debris. Pat each leg bone-dry with kitchen paper — use multiple pieces and press firmly. Any surface moisture will cause the duck fat to splatter dangerously when you submerge the legs, and will also prevent the skin from rendering properly. The legs can rest uncovered in the refrigerator for up to 2 hours at this stage if needed.

Melt the duck fat in a deep ovenproof casserole or heavy pot over low heat. Bring the fat to 90°C — use a thermometer; this temperature is non-negotiable. Gently submerge the dried duck legs, ensuring they are completely covered by fat. If the fat does not cover the legs, add more. Transfer to an oven preheated to 90°C (fan-assisted 80°C) and cook for 3 to 4 hours. The fat should barely quiver — no bubbles, no spattering. The legs are done when a thin metal skewer slides into the thigh with zero resistance and the flesh is pulling away from the bone by 5mm.

Remove the legs from the fat and let them drain on a wire rack for 5 minutes. Heat a heavy cast-iron or carbon-steel pan over medium-high heat until smoking. Place the legs skin-side down in the dry pan — no oil, the legs carry their own fat — and press them flat with a spatula or heavy pan. Sear for 4–6 minutes without moving until the skin is deep copper-brown, crisp, and blistered. Flip once and warm the flesh side for 1 minute only. Serve within minutes — the skin softens rapidly.
fr-eclairs: Heat the milk to a bare simmer. Whisk yolks, sugar, and cornstarch together in a bowl until pale and thick. Pour half the hot milk over the egg mixture, whisking constantly, then return everything to the saucepan. Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly with a whisk, until the cream boils and thickens — it must reach a full boil to fully cook out the cornstarch enzyme that causes it to thin again on cooling. Strain through a fine sieve into a clean bowl, press plastic wrap directly on the surface, and refrigerate until fully cold — minimum 2 hours.

Make pâte à choux: bring water, butter, and salt to a rolling boil, add all flour at once, stir vigorously until the dough pulls away from the pan and forms a dry film on the bottom (about 2 minutes over medium heat). Cool for 2 minutes, then beat in eggs one at a time until the dough falls from a spoon in a V-shaped ribbon. Fill a piping bag with a large plain tip (14mm). Pipe 12cm logs on a parchment-lined sheet, keeping the pipe absolutely level and consistent in pressure. Wet a finger and smooth any peaks.

Bake at 200°C (390°F) for 25 minutes without opening the oven — steam inside the shells is what causes the hollow cavity, and cold air will collapse them irreversibly. After 25 minutes, reduce to 170°C and bake 10 more minutes with the oven door slightly ajar to allow the steam to escape. The finished shells should be deep golden-brown, completely dry, hollow-sounding when tapped, and rigid. Pierce each end immediately with a skewer when they come out of the oven.

Whip the chilled pastry cream briefly until smooth. Fill a piping bag with a small plain tip (5mm). Insert the tip into one of the pierced ends of each éclair and pipe slowly, filling until cream just begins to emerge from the other end. The shell should feel noticeably heavier and the sides should resist gently when squeezed — a sign of even filling. Do not overfill — bulging shells look clumsy and risk cracking.

Make the glaze: heat the heavy cream to a simmer, pour over the chopped dark chocolate, wait 60 seconds, then stir from the center outward until completely smooth and glossy. Dip the top of each éclair into the glaze at a 45-degree angle, allowing excess to drip for 3–4 seconds. Run a clean finger along one edge of the dipped side to create a clean glaze line. Refrigerate for 20 minutes to set the glaze before serving. The glaze should set firm and crack cleanly when bitten.
